inasmuch.e: Univerbation of in + as + much ("to such a degree"), from Middle English in als mikel, a Northern form.
inasmuch.g: In like degree; in like manner; to the same or similar degree; likewise.

incapable.e: Borrowed from Middle French incapable, equivalent to in- + capable.

incense.e: From Middle English encens, from Old French encens (“sweet-smelling substance”) from Late Latin incensum (“burnt incense”, literally “something burnt”), neuter past participle of incendō (“to set on fire”).
incense.g: Biotic material that releases fragrant smoke when burnt, often used in religious rites or for aesthetic reasons.

incite.e: From Middle French inciter, from Latin incitō (“to set in motion, hasten, urge, incite”), from in (“in, on”) + citō (“to set in motion, urge”), frequentative of cieō (“to rouse, excite, call”).

inclination.e: From Middle English inclinacioun, inclinacyon, from Old French inclination and Latin inclīnātiō. Morphologically incline + -ation.

incline.e: From Middle English enclinen, from Old French encliner (modern incliner), from Latin inclīnō (“incline, tilt”), from in- + clīnō (compare -cline), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley- (English lean).
incline.g: To bend or move (something) out of a given plane or direction, often the horizontal or vertical.

include.e: From Middle English includen, borrowed from Latin inclūdere (“to shut in, enclose, insert”), from in- (“in”) + claudere (“to shut”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂w- (“key, hook, nail”).
include.g: To bring into a group, class, set, or total as a (new) part or member.

including.g: Such as, among which; introducing one or more parts of the group or topic just mentioned.

income.e: From Middle English income, perhaps continuing (in altered form) Old English incyme (“an in-coming, entrance”), equivalent to in- + come.
income.g: Money one earns by working or by capitalising on the work of others.

incomplete.e: From Middle English incomplete, incompleet, from Late Latin incomplētus, from in- (“un-; not”) + complētus (“complete”), equivalent to in- (“not”) + complete.

inconspicuous.e: Borrowed from Late Latin incōnspicuus. Equivalent to in- + conspicuous.

incontinency.e: From Middle English incontinency, from Latin incontinentia.

incontinent.e: From Middle English incontinent, from Old French incontinent, from Latin incontinens, from in + continens.

incorruptible.e: Borrowed from Middle French incorruptible, from Latin incorruptibilis. By surface analysis, in- + corruptible.
incorruptible.g: Incapable of being bribed or morally corrupted; inflexibly just and upright.

increase.e: From Middle English encresen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman encreistre, from Latin increscere (“to increase”), from in (“in, on”) + crescō (“grow”).
increase.g: (of a quantity, etc.) To become larger or greater, to greaten.

increasingly.e: From Middle English encreessingli, equivalent to increasing + -ly.

incredible.e: From Middle English incredible, from Latin incrēdibilis (“that cannot be believed”), from in- (“not”) + crēdibilis (“worthy of belief”), from crēdō (“believe”), equivalent to in- + credible.
incredible.g: Too implausible to be credible; beyond belief.

incur.e: From Middle English incurren, from Anglo-Norman encurir, Middle French encourir, from Old French encorre, from Latin incurrere.
incur.g: To bring upon oneself or expose oneself to, especially something inconvenient, harmful, or onerous; to become liable or subject to.

incurable.e: From Old French incurable, from Late Latin incurabilis.
incurable.g: Of an illness, condition, etc, that is unable to be cured; healless.

indebt.e: From Middle English endetten, Old French endetter, from en- + detter, from dette (“debt”), by surface analysis, in- + debt.
indebt.g: To bring into debt; to place under obligation.

indecency.g: Lack of decency; the property or degree of being indecent.

indecision.g: The inability to decide on a course of action, especially if two or more possibilities exist.

indeed.e: From Middle English indede, univerbation of the phrase in dede (“in sooth, in fact”). By surface analysis, in + deed.

independent.e: From Middle English independent, equivalent to in- + dependent.
independent.g: Not dependent; not contingent or depending on something else; free.

indicate.e: Borrowed from Latin indicātus, perfect passive participle of indicō (“to point out, indicate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“in, to”) + dicō (“to declare, (originally) to point”).
indicate.g: To point out; to discover; to direct to a knowledge of; to show; to make known.

indict.e: From Middle English enditen, endyten (“to accuse”), from Old French enditer (“to dictate, indite”), from Late Latin indictāre, frequentative of Latin indicere (“to proclaim”), from in- + dicere (“to say”), or from in- + dictāre (“to say often, to dictate”).

indictment.e: 18th-century Latinized respelling of Middle English endytement (“action of accusing”), from Anglo-Norman enditement, from enditer, from Late Latin indictāre, from Latin indictus.
indictment.g: An official formal accusation for a criminal offence, or the process by which it is brought to a jury.

indignant.e: Borrowed from Latin indignāns, present participle of indignor (“to consider as unworthy, be angry or displeased at”), from in- (“privative”) + dignor (“to deem worthy”), from dignus (“worthy”).
indignant.g: Showing anger or indignation, especially at something unjust or wrong.

indignation.e: From Middle English indignacioun, borrowed from Old French indignation, from Latin indignātiō, from indignor (“to scorn, resent”), from indignus (“unworthy, not fitting”), from in- (“not”) + dignus (“worthy, appropriate”).
indignation.g: An anger aroused by something perceived as an indignity, notably an offense or injustice.

indiscretion.e: From Old French, from Late Latin indiscrētiō.
indiscretion.g: The quality or state of being indiscreet; lack of discretion

indispensable.e: Borrowed from Middle French indispensable, from Medieval Latin indispensābilis, corresponding to in- + dispensable.
indispensable.g: Absolutely necessary or requisite; that one cannot do without.

indisputably.e: From indisputable + -ly. By surface analysis, in- + disputably.
indisputably.g: In a manner that is incapable of being disputed or argued against.

indite.e: Originally a variant of indict; from Middle English enditen, endyten, from Old French enditer, from Late Latin indictāre, from in- + dictare (“to declare”).
indite.g: To physically make (letters and words) on a writing surface; to inscribe.
An extremely rare indium-iron sulfide mineral.

individual.e: From Medieval Latin indīviduālis, from Latin indīviduum (“an indivisible thing”), neuter of indīviduus (“indivisible, undivided”), from in + dīviduus (“divisible”), from dīvidō (“divide”).
individual.g: A person considered alone, rather than as belonging to a group of people.

indulge.g: To yield to a temptation or desire.

indulgence.e: From Middle English indulgence, indulgens, from Middle French indulgence and its source, Latin indulgentia.

industrious.e: From Middle French industrieux, from Late Latin industriosus (“diligent, active, industrious”), from Latin industria (“diligence, industry”); see industry.

inevitable.e: From Middle French inevitable, from Latin inēvītābilis (“unavoidable”), from in- + ēvītābilis (“avoidable”), from ēvītāre (“to avoid”), from ē- (“out”) + vītāre (“to shun”).

inexcusable.e: From Middle French inexcusable, from Latin inexcusabilis.

inexpressible.e: From in- + expressible. Piecewise doublet of unexpressible.
inexpressible.g: Unable to be expressed; not able to be put into words.

infallible.e: From Medieval Latin īnfallibilis, from Latin in- + fallibilis. By surface analysis, in- + fallible.
infallible.g: A person who, or an object or process that, is taken as being infallible.

infamous.e: From Middle English enfamouse, in-fames, infamous, from Medieval Latin īnfāmōsus, from Latin īnfāmis; by surface analysis, in- + famous.
infamous.g: Having a bad reputation; disreputable; notorious; unpleasant or evil; widely known, especially for something scornful.

infamy.e: From late Middle English infamie, from Old French infamie, from Latin īnfāmia (“infamy”), from īnfāmis (“infamous”), from in- (“not”) + fāma (“fame, renown”).

infancy.e: From Middle English infancie, from Latin īnfantia (“infancy, early childhood; childishness”), equivalent to infant + -cy.
infancy.g: The earliest period of childhood (crawling rather than walking).

infant.e: From Middle English infaunt, borrowed from Latin īnfantem, accusative masculine singular of īnfāns, nominal use of the adjective meaning 'not able to speak', from īn- (“not”) + fāns, present participle of for (“to speak”).
infant.g: A very young human being, from birth to somewhere between six months and two years of age after birth, needing almost constant care and atte

infect.e: From Middle French infect, from Latin infectus, perfect passive participle of inficiō (“dye, taint”).
infect.g: To bring (the body or part of it) into contact with a substance that causes illness (a pathogen), so that the pathogen begins to act on the

infect.e: Borrowed from Latin īnfectus, equivalent to in- (“not”) + factus, perfect passive participle of faciō (“to do, make”).
infect.g: Representing an action not yet completed.

infection.e: From Old French infection, from Late Latin īnfectiō. Equivalent to infect + -ion.
infection.g: The act or process of infecting.

infectious.e: Borrowed from New Latin īnfectiōsus. By surface analysis, infect + -ious.
infectious.g: Caused by an agent that enters the host's body (such as a bacterium, virus, parasite, or prion); often, also, transmitted among hosts via an

inferior.e: Borrowed from Latin īnferior (“lower in situation or place”), comparative of īnferus (“below, underneath”).
inferior.g: Lower in rank, status, or quality.

infest.e: From Middle English infesten, from Old French infester (“to infest”), from Latin īnfestō (“assail, molest”, verb), from īnfestus (“hostile”), of uncertain origin.
infest.g: To inhabit a place in unpleasantly large numbers; to plague, harass.

infidelity.e: From Middle English infidelite, from Middle French infidelité (modern French infidélité) and its etymon Latin īnfidēlitās. Equivalent to infidel + -ity.
infidelity.g: Unfaithfulness in a marriage or an intimate (sexual or romantic) relationship: practice or instance of having a sexual or romantic affair wi

infinite.e: From Middle English infinite, from Old French infinit and its etymon Latin īnfīnītus, from in- (“not”) + fīnis (“end”) + the perfect passive participle ending -ītus. By surface analysis, in- + finite.

inflame.e: From Middle English inflammen, enflamen, enflaumen (“to set (something) on fire; to be on fire; (figurative) to enrage (someone); to become enraged; to incite (someone) to do evil; to inspire (someone); (medicine) to cause inflammation of (a body part)”), from Old French enflamer, enflammer (“to set (something) on fire, inflame; to be on fire.
inflame.g: To set (someone or something) on fire; to cause (someone or something) to burn, flame, or glow; to kindle.

inflammation.e: From Middle French inflammation, from Latin īnflammātiō, equivalent to inflame + -ation.
inflammation.g: The act of inflaming, kindling, or setting on fire.

inflict.e: From Latin īnflīctus, from in- + flīctus, past participle of īnflīgō (“to knock or strike against”), from in- + flīgō (“strike”).

inflow.e: From Middle English inflowen, equivalent to in- + flow.
inflow.g: The act or process of flowing in or into.

influence.e: From Middle English influence, from Old French influence, a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin īnfluentia, from Latin īnfluēns + -ia.
influence.g: The power to affect, control or manipulate something or someone; the ability to change the development of fluctuating things such as conduct

infold.e: From Middle English infolden, equivalent to in- + fold.

inform.e: From Middle English informen, enformen, borrowed from Old French enformer, informer (“to train, instruct, inform”), from Latin īnfōrmō (“to shape, form, train, instruct, educate”), from in- (“into”) + fōrma (“form, shape”), equivalent to in- + form.
inform.g: To instruct, train (usually in matters of knowledge).
Without regular form; shapeless; ugly; deformed.

information.e: From Middle English enformacioun, informacioun, borrowed from Anglo-Norman informacioun, enformation, Old French information, from Latin īnfōrmātiō (“formation, conception; education”), from the participle stem of īnformāre (“to inform”). Equivalent to inform + -ation.
information.g: Something that provides a definitive characterization or description of the nature and attributes of a specified entity.

informed.g: Instructed; having knowledge of a fact or area of education.

ingather.e: From Middle English ingaderen (“To drive (enemy troops) into a trap”), equivalent to in- + gather.

inhabit.e: From Old French enhabiter, from Latin inhabitāre (in + habitāre).

inhabitant.e: From Middle English inhabitantes (n. plural) and inhabitaunt (adj.), from Old French inhabitant, from Latin inhabitāns, present participle of inhabitō (“to inhabit”), from in- (“in”) + habitō (“to dwell”) (frequentative of habeō (“to hold”), from Proto-Indo-European *ghabh- (“to seize, take, hold, have”). By surface analysis, inhabit + -ant.
inhabitant.g: Someone or thing who lives in a place.

inherit.e: From Middle English enheriten, from Old French enheriter, from Late Latin inhereditare (“make heir”).
inherit.g: To receive (property, a title, etc.), by legal succession or bequest, usually after the previous owner's death.

inheritance.e: From Middle English enheritaunce, inheritaunce, borrowed from Anglo-Norman, Old French enheritaunce, from enheriter. By surface analysis, inherit + -ance.
inheritance.g: The passing of title to an estate upon death.

inheritor.e: From Middle English enheriter, enheritour. By surface analysis, inherit + -or.
inheritor.g: Someone who inherits something; an heir.

iniquity.e: From Middle English iniquite, jniquite (“evil, wickedness, iniquity; evil act; hostility, malevolence; hostile act; a calamity, misfortune”), from Old French iniquité (modern French iniquité (“iniquity”)), from Latin inīquitās (“iniquity; inequality, unfairness; inequity, injustice”), from inīquus (“unequal, uneven, unfair; disadvantageous, unfavourable.
iniquity.g: Deviation from what is right; gross injustice, sin, wickedness.

initial.e: From Middle French initial or directly from its Latin etymon initiālis (“of the beginning, incipient, initial”), from initium (“a going in, entrance”), from inīre (“to go into, enter”), from in (“in”) + ire (“to go”).
initial.g: Chronologically first, early; of or pertaining to the beginning, cause or origin.

injure.e: A back-formation from injury, from Middle English injurie, from Anglo-Norman injurie, from Latin iniūria (“injustice; wrong; offense”), from in- (“not”) + iūs, iūris (“right, law”).
injure.g: To wound or cause physical harm to a living creature.

injurious.e: From Middle English injurious, from Anglo-Norman enjurius, from Latin iniūriōsus; analysable as injury + -ous.
injurious.g: Causing physical harm or injury; harmful, hurtful.

injury.e: From Middle English injurie, from Anglo-Norman injurie, from Latin iniūria (“injustice; wrong; offense”), from in- (“not”) + iūs, iūris (“right, law”).
injury.g: Damage to the body of a living thing.

injustice.e: From Middle English injustice, from Old French injustice, from Latin iniustitia. Equivalent to in- + justice.

ink.e: From Middle English ynke, from Old French enque, from Latin encaustum (“purple ink used by Roman emperors to sign documents”), from Ancient Greek ἔγκαυστον (énkauston, “burned-in”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + καίω (kaíō, “burn”). In this sense, displaced native Old English blæc (“ink”, literally “black”). Sense four refers to the ink used in newspapers.
ink.g: A pigment (or dye)-based fluid used for writing, printing etc.

inkhorn.e: From Middle English ynkhorn, inkehorn (“small portable vessel, originally made of horn, used to hold ink”), equivalent to ink + horn.
inkhorn.g: A small portable container, often made of horn, used to carry ink.

inland.e: From Middle English inland, inlond, from Old English inland, equivalent to in- + land.
inland.g: Within the land; relatively remote from the ocean or from open water; interior.

inmost.e: From Middle English inmost, from Old English innemest, a double superlative form from inne (“within”), from in (“in”). The modern form is due to confusion with most.
inmost.g: That which is inmost; the core.

inn.e: From Middle English in, inn, from Old English inn (“a dwelling, house, chamber, lodging”); akin to Icelandic inni (“a dwelling place, home, abode”), Faroese inni (“home”).
inn.g: Any establishment where travellers can procure lodging, food, and drink.

inner.e: From Middle English inner, ynner, ynnere, from Old English innera, comparative of inne (“within”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁en.
inner.g: Being or occurring (farther) inside, situated farther in, located (situated) or happening on the inside of something, situated within or far

innermost.e: From Middle English innermost, innermest, in-nermast, alteration (due to Middle English inner, innere (“inner”)) of Old English innemest (“innermost”), equivalent to inner + -most.
innermost.g: That which is innermost; the core.

innkeeper.e: From Middle English inkeper; equivalent to inn + keeper.
innkeeper.g: The person responsible for the running of an inn, usually the proprietor.

innocence.e: From Middle English innocence, from Old French innocence, inocence, from Latin innocentia.
innocence.g: Absence of responsibility for a crime, tort, etc.

innocency.e: From Middle English innocencie, from Latin innocentia.

innocent.e: From Middle English innocent, from Old French innocent, inocent, borrowed from Latin innocēns (“harmless, inoffensive”), from in- (“not”) + nocēns, present participle of noceō (“to hurt”). By surface analysis, in- (“not”) + nocent (“harmful; guilty”).
innocent.g: Free from guilt, sin, or immorality.

innumerable.e: From in- + numerable; from Middle English innumerable, from Latin innumerābilis, from in- + numerābilis.
innumerable.g: Not capable of being counted, enumerated, or numbered.

inordinate.e: From Middle English inordinat, from Latin inōrdinātus (“not arranged, disordered, irregular”), from in- + ordinatus, past participle of ōrdināre (“to arrange, order”).
inordinate.g: Excessive; unreasonable or inappropriate in magnitude.

inquire.e: From Latin inquīrō (“to seek for”), composed of in- (“in, at, on; into”) + quaerō (“to seek, look for”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Italic *kʷaizeō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂- (“to acquire”).

inquiry.e: From Middle English enquery, from the Old French verb enquerre, from Latin inquīrō, composed of in- (“in, at, on; into”) + quaerō (“to seek, look for”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Italic *kʷaizeō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂- (“to acquire”).
inquiry.g: The act of inquiring; a seeking of information by asking questions; interrogation; a question or questioning.

inquisition.e: From Old French inquisicion, from Latin inquisitio, from inquirere. The sense implying persecution is influenced by the name of the Spanish Inquisition, which is a cardinal exemplar of government inquisitions that give inquisitions a bad name.
inquisition.g: An inquiry or investigation into the truth of some matter.

insane.e: From Latin īnsānus (“unsound in mind; mad, insane”), from in- + sānus (“sound, sane”), equivalent to in- + sane.
insane.g: Exhibiting unsoundness or disorder of mind; not sane; utterly mad.

inscribe.e: Borrowed from Latin īnscrībō, from in- (“upon”) and scrībō (“to write”).
inscribe.g: To write or cut (words) onto (something, especially a hard surface, or a book to be given to another person); to engrave.

insect.e: Borrowed from Middle French insecte, from Latin īnsectum, from īnsectus (“cut into, cut up, with a notched or divided body”), from perfect passive participle of īnsecō (“to cut into, to cut up”), from in- + secō (“to cut”), from the notion that the insect's body is "cut into" three sections (head, thorax, abdomen).
insect.g: An arthropod (in the Insecta class) characterized by six legs, up to four wings, and a chitinous exoskeleton.

insert.e: From Latin insertus, past participle of inserō, from in- + serō (“join, bind together, connect, entwine, interweave”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to bind, put together, to line up”).
insert.g: To put in between or into.

inside.e: From Middle English ynneside; equivalent to in- + side.

insight.e: From Middle English insight, insiht (“insight, mental vision, intelligence, understanding”), equivalent to in- + sight. Perhaps continuing Old English insiht (“narrative, argument, account”), from Proto-Germanic *insahtiz (“account, narrative, argument”).
insight.g: A sight or view of the interior of anything; a deep inspection or view; introspection; frequently used with into.

insignificant.g: Not significant; not important, inconsequential, or having no noticeable effect.

insist.e: Partly from Middle French insister, from Latin īnsistere; and partly from a back-formation from insistence.
insist.g: To hold up a claim emphatically.

insistent.e: From Latin insistens, participle of insisto.

insolence.e: From Middle French insolence, from Latin īnsolentia.
insolence.g: Contemptible, ill-mannered conduct; insulting: arrogant, bold behaviour or attitude.

insolent.e: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin īnsolēns (“unaccustomed, unwanted, unusual, immoderate, excessive, arrogant, insolent”), from in- (privative prefix) + solēns, present participle of solēre (“to be accustomed, to be wont”).
insolent.g: Insulting in manner or words, particularly in an arrogant or insubordinate manner.

insomuch.e: From Middle English insomuche; equivalent to in + so + much.
insomuch.g: Because of; since; as a result of.

inspect.e: From Latin inspectum, past participle of inspicere (“to look into”), from in (“in”) + specere (“to look at”), equivalent to in- + -spect.
inspect.g: To examine critically or carefully; especially, to search out problems or determine condition; to scrutinize.

inspection.e: From Middle French, from Old French inspeccion, from Latin īnspectiō (“examination, inspection”), from the verb īnspiciō (“to inspect”), from speciō (“to look at”). By surface analysis, inspect + -ion.
inspection.g: The act of examining something, often closely.

inspiration.e: From Middle English inspiracioun, from Old French inspiration, from Late Latin īnspīrātiōnem (nominative: īnspīrātiō), from Latin īnspīrātus (past participle of inspīrō). By surface analysis, inspire + -ation.
inspiration.g: The drawing of air into the lungs, accomplished in mammals by elevation of the chest walls and flattening of the diaphragm, as part of the a

inspire.e: From Middle English inspiren, enspiren, from Old French inspirer, variant of espirer, from Latin īnspīrāre (“inspire”), itself a loan-translation of Biblical Ancient Greek πνέω (pnéō, “breathe”), from in + spīrō (“breathe”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)peys- (“to blow, breathe”).
inspire.g: To infuse into the mind; to communicate to the spirit; to convey, as by a divine or supernatural influence; to disclose preternaturally; to

install.e: From Middle English installen, from Old French installer, from Medieval Latin īnstallō (“to install, put in place, establish”), from in- + stallum (“stall”), from Frankish *stall (“stall, position, place”), from Proto-Germanic *stallaz (“place, position”), from Proto-Indo-European *stel-, *stAlǝn-, *stAlǝm- (“stem, trunk”).
install.g: To connect, set up or prepare something for use

instance.e: Borrowed from Middle French instance, from Latin īnstantia (“a being near, presence, also perseverance, earnestness, importunity, urgency”), from īnstāns (“urgent”); see instant.
instance.g: Urgency of manner or words; an urgent request; insistence.

instant.e: From Middle English instant (“infinitely short period of time”), from Old French instant (“assiduous, at hand”, adjective), from Latin īnstāns, īnstantis (“present, pressing, urgent”, literally “standing near”), present active participle of īnstō (“to stand upon, be nearby”), from in- (“after”) + stō (“to stand”).
instant.g: A very short period of time; a moment.

instant.e: Ultimately from Latin īnstāre; its precise evolution is uncertain. OED hints at (unattested) Middle French *instanter.
instant.g: To urge, press (someone); to insist on, demand (something).

instead.e: From in + stead, from Middle English ine (“in”) + stede (“stead”).
instead.g: In the place of something (usually mentioned earlier); as a substitute or alternative.

instinct.e: From Latin īnstīnctus, past participle of īnstinguō (“to incite, to instigate”), from in (“in, on”) + stinguō (“to prick”).
instinct.g: A natural or inherent impulse or behaviour.

institution.e: From Middle English institucioun, from Old French institution, from Latin institūtiō, from instituō (“to set up”), from in- (“in, on”) + statuō (“to set up, establish”). Equivalent to institute + -ion.
institution.g: A long-established organization or type of organization, particularly one involved with education, public service, or charity work.

instruct.e: From Latin īnstrūctus, perfect passive participle of īnstruō (“I instruct; I arrange, furnish, or provide”).

instruction.e: From Middle English instruccioun, from Old French instruccion, from Latin instructio; equivalent to instruct + -ion.
instruction.g: The act of instructing, teaching, or providing with information or knowledge.

instructor.e: From Latin instructor, equivalent to instruct + -or.

instrument.e: From Middle English instrument, from Old French instrument, from Latin īnstrūmentum (“an implement, tool”), From īnstruō (“build, construct; arrange”) + -mentum.
instrument.g: A device used to produce music.

insubordinate.e: From in- + subordinate, on model of French insubordonné.
insubordinate.g: Rebellious or defiant to authority; contumacious.

insubordination.e: From in- + subordination, on the model of French insubordination.
insubordination.g: The quality or state of being insubordinate; disobedience to lawful authority; specifically, an employee's failure or refusal to comply with

insurrection.e: From Late Middle English insurreccion (“uprising against a government, rebellion, revolt; civil disorder, riot; illegal armed assault”), from Middle French insurrection, Old French insurreccïon (modern French insurrection), and from their etymon Latin īnsurrēctiōnem (rare), the accusative singular of īnsurrēctiō (“rising up, insurrection, rebellion”).
insurrection.g: The action of part or all of a national population violently rising up against the government or other authority; (countable) an instance of

intact.e: From Middle French intact, from Latin intact(us).
intact.g: Left complete or whole; not touched, defiled, sullied, or otherwise damaged.

integrity.e: Borrowed from Middle French intégrité, from Latin integritās (“soundness, integrity”), from integer.
integrity.g: Steadfast adherence to a strict moral or ethical code.

intelligence.e: From Middle English intelligence, from Old French intelligence, from Latin intelligentia, which is most likely from inter- (“between”) + legere (“to choose, pick out, read”).
intelligence.g: The capacity of mind, especially to understand principles, truths, facts or meanings, acquire knowledge, and apply it to practice; the abili

intelligent.e: From Middle French intelligent, from Latin intellegēns (“discerning”), present active participle of intellegō (“understand, comprehend”), itself from inter (“between”) + legō (“choose, pick out, read”).
intelligent.g: Of high or especially quick cognitive capacity, bright.

intelligent.e: Partly from Russian интеллиге́нт (intelligént) and partly from the adjective.
intelligent.g: A member of the intelligentsia; an intelligent person.

intelligible.e: From Middle French intelligible, from Old French, from Latin intelligibilis.
intelligible.g: Capable of being understood; clear to the mind.

intend.e: From Middle English intenden, entenden (“direct (one’s) attention towards”), borrowed from Old French entendre, from Latin intendō, intendere. Largely displaced native Old English myntan (“to mean, intend; to think, suppose”), whence dialectal mint.
intend.g: To fix the mind upon (something, or something to be accomplished); be intent upon

intense.e: From Late Middle English intens, intense (“ardent, fervent; extreme, great, intense”), borrowed from Old French intense (modern French intense), or directly from its etymon Latin intēnsus (“strained, stretched tight; intense; attentive; violent; (rare) eager, intent”), the perfect passive participle of intendō (“to stretch out, strain”).
intense.g: Of a characteristic: extreme or very high or strong in degree; severe; also, excessive, towering.

intent.e: Existing since Middle English entente, from Old French entent or entente, ultimately from Latin intentus. Modified later in spelling to align more closely with the Latin word.

intention.e: From Middle English entencioun, intention, from Old French entencion, from Latin intentiō, intentiōnem. Equivalent to intent + -ion.
intention.g: A course of action that a person intends to follow.

intercede.e: From Middle French intercéder, from Latin intercēdō, from inter- (“between”) + cēdō (“I go”) (English cede), literally “to (act as) go-between”.
intercede.g: To plead on someone else's behalf.

intercession.e: From Middle French intercession, from Old French intercession, from Latin intercessiō, from intercēdō, from inter- (“between”) + cēdō (“to go”) (English cede), literally “go-between”.
intercession.g: The act of intervening or mediating between two parties.

intercessor.e: Late 15th century, from Latin intercessor, from Latin intercēdō, from inter (“between”) + cēdō (“to go”) (English cede), literally “go-between”.

interest.e: From Middle English interest, from Old French interesse and interest (French intérêt), from Medieval Latin interesse, from Latin interesse.
interest.g: The price paid for obtaining, or price received for providing, money or goods in a credit transaction, calculated as a fraction of the amoun

interfere.e: From Old French entreferir, from entre- + ferir (“to hit, to strike”), itself from the Latin verb ferio.
interfere.g: To get involved or involve oneself, causing disturbance.

interior.g: Within any limits, enclosure, or substance; inside; internal; inner.

intermeddle.e: From Middle English entremedlen, entermedlen, from Anglo-Norman entremedler (= Old French entremesler), from inter- + medler.

intermission.e: From Latin intermissiō, from intermittō (“interrupt, omit”) + -tiō.
intermission.g: A break, especially between two performances or sessions, such as at a concert, play, seminar, or religious assembly.

interpret.e: From Middle English interpreten, from Old French enterpreter, (French interpréter), from Latin interpretor (“to explain, expound, interpret”), past participle interpretatus, from interpres (“an agent, broker, explainer, interpreter, negotiator”), from inter (“between”) + -pres, probably the root of pretium (“price”).
interpret.g: To decode the meaning of a topic and then act, whether to continue researching the topic, follow through, act in opposition, or further the

interpretation.e: From Middle English interpretacioun, from the Anglo-Norman form of Old French interpretacion, from Latin interpretātiō, noun of action from interpretor (“to explain, expound, interpret, understand, conclude, infer, comprehend”). Morphologically interpret + -ation.
interpretation.g: An act of interpreting or explaining something unclear; a translation; a version.

interpreter.e: From Middle English interpreter, interpretour, etc., from Old French interpreteur, interpreteeur, etc., from Late Latin interpretātōr, from classical Latin interpretātus (“explained, translated”) + -or (“-er: forming agent nouns”), from interpretārī (“to explain, to translate”), from interpres (“go-between, translator”) + -ārī (“to be ~ed”), q.v.
interpreter.g: A person or thing that interprets the meaning of something for another, particularly

interrogate.e: Borrowed from Latin interrogātus, the perfect passive participle of Latin interrogō (“to inquire, interrogate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
interrogate.g: To question or quiz, especially in a thorough or aggressive manner.

intervene.e: Back-formation from intervention, and/or from Latin interveniō (“come between”, verb).
intervene.g: To become involved in a situation, so as to alter or prevent an action.

intestine.e: From Latin intestīnum, neuter of intestīnus (“internal”), as Etymology 2, below.
intestine.g: The alimentary canal of an animal through which food passes after having passed all stomachs.
Domestic; taking place within a given country or region.

intimidate.e: From Medieval Latin intimidātus, perfect passive participle of Latin intimidō (“to intimidate, terrify”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + timidus (“afraid, timid”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix); see timid.
intimidate.g: To make timid or afraid; to cause to feel fear or nervousness; to deter, especially by threats of violence.

intolerable.e: From Middle English intolerable, borrowed from Middle French intolerable, from Latin intolerābilis. By surface analysis, in- + tolerable.
intolerable.g: Not tolerable; not capable of being borne or endured.

intoxicate.g: To stupefy by doping with chemical substances such as alcohol.

intrigue.e: Borrowed from French intrigue, from Italian intricare, from Latin intrīcō (“to entangle, perplex, embarrass”).
intrigue.g: A complicated or clandestine plot or scheme intended to effect some purpose by secret artifice; conspiracy; stratagem; the practice of engag

introduce.e: From Middle English introducen, from Old French introduire, from Latin intrōdūcō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁énteros (“inner, what is inside”) and *dewk-.
introduce.g: To cause (someone) to be acquainted (with someone else).

intrude.e: From Latin intrudere, from in- + trudere (“to thrust”).
intrude.g: To thrust oneself in; to come or enter without invitation, permission, or welcome; to encroach; to trespass.

invalid.e: Borrowed from Middle French invalide, from Latin invalidus (“infirm, weak”), from in- (“not”) + validus (“strong”).
invalid.g: Any person with a disability or illness.

invasion.e: From Middle French invasion, from Late Latin invāsiōnem, accusative of invāsiō.
invasion.g: A military action consisting of a large armed force of one geopolitical entity entering territory controlled by another such entity, general

invent.e: From Middle English inventen, borrowed from Old French inventer, from Latin inventus, perfect passive participle of inveniō (“come upon, meet with, find, discover”), from in (“in, on”) + veniō (“come”); see venture.
invent.g: To design a new process or mechanism.

invention.e: From Middle English invencion, invencioun, from Latin inventiō either directly or via Middle French invencion, from Latin invenīre (“to discover, find, invent”), from in- (“in-: in, into”) + venīre (“to come”). By surface analysis, invent + -ion.

inventor.e: Borrowed from Latin inventor. By surface analysis, invent + -or.
inventor.g: One who invents, either as a hobby or as an occupation.

inventory.e: From Middle English inventorie, from Medieval Latin inventōrium, alteration of Late Latin inventārium, from Latin inveniō (“to find out”).
inventory.g: The stock of an item on hand at a particular location or business.

investigate.e: Recorded since circa 1510, a back-formation from investigation on the basis of -ate (verb-forming suffix), from Latin investīgātiō (“a searching into”), from investīgātus, the perfect passive participle of investīgō, equivalent to in- + vestigate.
investigate.g: To inquire into or study in order to ascertain facts or information.

investigation.e: From Middle English investigacioun, from Old French investigacion, from Latin investigatio. Morphologically investigate + -ion.
investigation.g: The act of investigating; the process of inquiring into or following up; research, especially patient or thorough inquiry or examination

invisible.e: From Middle English invisible, from Old French invisible, from Late Latin invīsibilis. Morphologically in- + visible. Piecewise doublet of unvisible.
invisible.g: Unable to be seen; out of sight; not visible.

invite.e: From Middle French inviter, from Latin invītō.
invite.g: To ask for the presence or participation of someone or something.

invoke.e: From Middle English *invoken, envoken, borrowed from Old French envoquer, from Latin invocāre (“to call upon”), itself from in- + vocare (“to call”).
invoke.g: To call upon (a person, a god) for help, assistance or guidance.

involve.e: From Late Middle English involven (“to cloud; to encumber; to envelop, surround; to ponder (something); (reflexive) to concern (oneself) with something”), borrowed from Old French involver, envoudre, or from its etymon Latin involvere, the present active infinitive of Latin involvō (“to roll to or upon something; to roll about; to coil or curl up; to cover.
involve.g: To have (something) as a component or a related part; to comprise, to include.

inward.e: From Middle English inward, from Old English inweard, corresponding to in + -ward.
inward.g: Situated on the inside; that is within, inner; belonging to the inside.
